However, achieving a low-complexity decoding was at the expense of a large gap between\\nthe code rate and the channel capacity.\\nThe discovery of Turbo codes in 1993 [3], which substantially decreased the gap to the\\ncapacity, started a new paradigm in the design of codes. This was followed by the rediscovery\\nof low-density parity-check (LDPC) and graph-based codes, which were originally introduced\\nby Gallager in the 1960’s [4] and include Turbo codes as a subclass, demonstrating that they can\\npractically achieve the channel capacity [5], [6] using low-complexity suboptimal decoders. The\\nkey to the success of Turbo and LDPC codes is that they both combine randomness and large\\ncode length, which were the main ingredients in proving the achievability of the capacity, with\\nsparsity and combinatorial structure, which enables low-complexity iterative decoding of long\\ncodes. Since then, much of the focus of coding theory has been on the design, decoding, and\\nanalysis of graph-based codes.\\n1.1.2 Graph-Based Codes\\nAny linear code can be described as the null space of a parity-check matrix, in a finite\\nfield. In other words, a code can be defined as the set of all vectors that satisfy a set of finite-field\\nlinear constraints, called the parity-check constraints. The parity-check matrix is not unique, and\\nany code has several equivalent parity-check representations.\\nOnce a noisy version of the transmitted codeword is recieved at the destination, an\\noptimal decoder tries, in rough terms, to find a vector that most resembles the received vector,\\namong all the valid codewords; i.e., those which satisfy all the parity-check constraints. For\\nan arbitrary linear code, finding this vector is NP-hard. In his proposal of LDPC codes [4],\\nGallager’s idea was that, if the parity-check constraints are sparse, i.e., each involve only a few\\nentries of the codeword, one can start from the observed vector, and modify it to satisfy the\\nparity-check constraints iteratively. In a graphical representation of the parity-check constraints,\\nthis is done by exchanging messages between the nodes, until all or the most possible number\\nof constraints are satisfied. This idea lead to the more recent development of a variety of iter-\\native message-passing (IMP) algorithms for decoding, including the sum-product and min-sum\\nalgorithms [7]. These algorithms are closely related to the iterative algorithms used in machine\\nlearning for inference on graphical models.\\nThe behavior of the error probability of LDPC codes as a function of the signal to\\nnoise ratio (SNR) typically consists of three important regions: At SNR values below a certain\\n\\n6\\ncode density.\\nIn Chapter 4, we make some steps toward designing an efficient LP solver by taking\\nadvantage of the structure inherent in the decoding problem. The LP solver we propose is based\\non a sparse implementation of the interior-point method, which is proven to converge in a num-\\nber of iterations that grows sub-logarithmically with the code length. The complexity of each\\niteration of the interior-point method is dominated by the calculation of the Newton step, which\\nis obtained by solving an (often ill-conditioned) system of linear equations. We show that, for the\\nLP subproblems in adaptive LP decoding, these systems of linear equations have a structure that\\ncan be exploited in order to solve them by a low-complexity iterative technique.
